Chronology 8 — Muhammad and the Seal of Prophethood

The storyline now reaches the claim that closes it on the Islamic side: Muhammad as the final prophet, allegedly foretold in the Bible.

The Qur'an's text

  • Muhammad is "the seal of the prophets" (Q 33:40).
  • He is said to be found "written with them in the Torah and the Gospel" (Q 7:157), and Jesus foretells a messenger "whose name is Ahmad" (Q 61:6).

The alleged biblical foreshadowings (Muslim reading)

  1. Deut 18:15–18 — "a prophet like Moses from among their brethren" → read as the Ishmaelite/Arab line.
  2. John 14:16,26; 15:26; 16:7 — the Paraclete → read as Ahmad (the paraklētos → periklytos "praised one" theory).
  3. *Deut 33:2 (Paran); Isa 29:12 ("he is not learned"); Song 5:16 (maḥamaddim); Hag 2:7* — assorted prooftexts.

The strongest Muslim case — stated fully

Fairness (and symmetry with the Abraham chapter) requires the best version, not a strawman:

  • Deut 18:18 "like Moses": the apologetic (Deedat and others) argues Jesus is unlike Moses (virgin-born, divine claims, no new legal code, no statecraft, did not die of old age) while Muhammad is more "like Moses" (ordinary birth and death, a law, leadership, warfare). On this reading "from among their brethren" points to the Ishmaelite cousins of Israel.
  • The Paraclete: Jesus promises "another Paraclete" (John 14:16), one who "will not speak on his own but what he hears" (John 16:13) — argued to resemble a man receiving revelation rather than an indwelling Spirit; with the periklytos ≈ Aḥmad word-play layered on top.
  • A real fairness point: the historicity of Muhammad himself is not in doubt — mainstream historians (e.g. Sean Anthony) treat him as a securely attested 7th-c. figure. The dispute is only the biblical-prophecy claim, not his existence; popular Christian polemic that blurs the two is itself a methodological error.

The Christian / academic response

  • Deut 18 "brethren": in Deuteronomy's own usage "brethren" = fellow Israelites; and the NT applies "the prophet like Moses" to Jesus (Acts 3:22). The reading is grammatically possible but contextually weaker.
  • The Paraclete: the Greek is paraklētos ("Advocate/Comforter"), and the text self-identifies it as the Holy Spirit who would come soon and dwell in the disciples (John 14:17,26) — not a future Arabian prophet. The periklytos ("Ahmad") emendation has no manuscript support whatsoever — and by the dossier's own manuscript standard (cap. 02, cap. 06), a reading with zero manuscript attestation cannot be asserted as the text.
  • "Like Moses": Acts 3:22–23 (and the early church) explicitly applies the Deut 18 prophet to Jesus; "like Moses" can be matched or mismatched selectively to anyone, so the criterion is weak both ways; "brethren" in Deuteronomy's own idiom = Israelites.
  • "Another Paraclete": John 14:26 names it the Holy Spirit, 14:17 says it would indwell the disciples, and it is given at Pentecost (Acts 2) — soon, internal, non-audible, non-Arabian. The periklytos emendation has zero manuscript support.
  • *Song 5:16 (maḥamaddim) is a Hebrew intensive plural ("wholly desirable"), not a personal name; Isa 29:12 is a judgment metaphor on Judah; Hag 2:7 / Deut 33:2 are read messianically by Christians themselves. They rest on isolated words out of context*.

Reverse symmetry — the method cuts both ways

Honesty requires noting: the Christian use of Old-Testament messianic prophecy is also largely retrospective and typological (flagged already for Gen 3:15 and "Let Us" in cap. 10/ cap. 11). So "you read your prophet back into our text" is a charge each side can level. The decisive asymmetry is narrow but real: the Muslim Paraclete claim additionally requires a textual emendation with no manuscript witness — which fails the same evenly-applied rule that voided the Christian Comma Johanneum. The Deut 18 reading, by contrast, is contextual, not text-critical, and is therefore only weak, not baseless.

Arbiter verdict — Muhammad foretold?

Present. Islam: Muhammad is the foretold, final prophet. Christianity/ academy: the cited texts refer to Israelite prophecy, Jesus, or the Holy Spirit, and the periklytos theory is text-critically baseless.

Weigh.

  • As historical/textual claims: weak. The Paraclete-as-Ahmad reading has no manuscript basis (the very standard the dossier applied to the Comma Johanneum, applied evenly here); the Deut 18 reading is contextually disfavoured.
  • As faith claims: non-falsifiable. "These passages secretly point to Muhammad" cannot be disproved, but neither can it be evidenced — and unfalsifiable is not the same as supported (Methodology §1.4, §4).
  • Finality / "seal": a theological axiom, not a historical datum; it has no pre-Islamic documentary footprint.

Judge. Separate two things popular polemic conflates. (1) Did Muhammad exist / lead a 7th-c. movement? — yes, not in dispute, and the dossier credits this against lazy denialism. (2) Do the biblical texts foretell him? — the evidence is weak to negative: the Deut 18 reading is contextually weak (the NT itself assigns it to Jesus) but not text-critically baseless; the Paraclete-as-Aḥmad reading is baseless by the dossier's own evenly-applied manuscript rule — the very scalpel that cut the Christian Comma Johanneum. The remaining prooftexts are out-of-context single words. On the theological claim of finality ("seal"), the arbiter does not rule true/false (out of remit) but records it rests on doctrine, not documentary evidence. And the reverse-symmetry caveat stands: retrospective prophecy-reading is a habit of both traditions; the asymmetry here is specifically the needed-but-unattested textual emendation.
